title: What is ours
hook: our judgments, impulses, desires and aversions are ours; body, property, reputation and office are not (Enchiridion 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was enchiridion, the little book kept in the hand. Your line was keep it at hand.

Page one of the handbook is not a pep talk. It's a sorting job. Two piles: into the first goes everything that is really yours; into the second, everything else. No warm-up, no story, no promise. Epictetus seems to think that if this one sorting goes wrong, nothing else in the book will help, and if it goes right, the rest will start to make sense on its own. So before it says anything about living well, the handbook asks a plainer question: what is ours?
screen: `PAGE ONE: A SORTING JOB.` → `TWO PILES.` → `WHAT IS OURS?`

segments.voice: In George Long's translation of 1877, the handbook begins: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." In our power: our opinions, our impulses toward things, our desires, our aversions; in a word, whatever is our own doing. Not in our power: the body, property, reputation, office; whatever is not our own doing. Now look what's in the second pile. Your own body. Your good name. Your job. On a list of what's mine, those might come first. Epictetus says no: your body can get sick without asking you, your reputation lives in other people's heads, your job can be taken by a letter. What you do with all of it, how you judge it, what you reach for and what you push away, stays with you. Why it matters: the things in our power, he says, are free by nature; nothing can block them. The rest are weak, slavish, easily blocked, and belong to others. Treat the second pile as if it were the first, he warns, and you'll be frustrated, and you'll blame gods and people. Then the tool. When something harsh shows up, he suggests saying to it: you are an appearance, not necessarily the thing you seem. Then ask one question: is this in my power or not? If it isn't, be ready to say: it is nothing to me. That sounds cold at first, but Epictetus means something narrower. Not that it doesn't matter, but that it isn't where your work is. Your work starts here.
screen: `SOME THINGS ARE IN OUR POWER.` · `BODY, PROPERTY, NAME: NOT OURS.` · `FREE BY NATURE, OR EASILY BLOCKED.` · `ASK: IS THIS IN MY POWER?` · then, large: `START HERE.`

segments.voice: Draw a line down the middle of a page, or do it in your head. On the left, three things that are yours in Epictetus' sense, like how you'll speak to someone, what you'll aim at, what you'll let go of; on the right, three that aren't, like the weather, someone else's decision, how a test comes back. Read both lists slowly, then rest your eyes on the left side and breathe.
George Long, whose 1877 translation opens the handbook's first sorting: our judgments, impulses, desires and aversions, not our body, property, reputation or office. Today's word.
Your line: start here. One plain question, is this in my power, and the work begins on your side of it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often sort a worry into what is up to them and what isn't, sometimes on paper in two columns, and put their effort into the first.
